Because box $$2$$ has a lower friction coefficient, it tends to slide down the slope faster than box $$1.$$ This means box $$2$$ pulls box $$1$$ down the slope somewhat, so that the mutual acceleration of the connected boxes, $$a,$$ which we found in part (a), is faster than $$a_1,$$ the acceleration of box $$1$$ on its down. If we look at the difference, we get $$a - a_1 = \dfrac{g\sin\theta(m_1+m_2) - g\cos\theta(\mu_1m_1+\mu_2m_2)}{m_1+m_2} - g(\sin\theta - \mu_1 \cos\theta).$$ The extra force needed to create this extra acceleration comes from the tension $$T$$ in the rod, so $$T = m_1(a - a_1)$$

We can test this equation for plausibility in a few cases. For example, suppose $$\mu_2 = \mu_1.$$ Then the two boxes should slide with the same acceleration down the slope and the tension should drop to zero because neither box needs to pull on the other. This is indeed the case. You may also want to test cases such as $$m_2 \to 0$$ for plausibility.

If you had extra time and wanted to double-check the plausibility of your answer, you could repeat the above calculation for $$m_2$$ and confirm that it gives the same result.

Plugging in the given numbers, we obtain $$\boxed{T = 0.940 \;\mathrm{N}}.$$

**c)** The big idea this week was to solve problems in terms of variables. In this part, we see the power of this approach. When we examine the answer to part (a), we see that the masses only ever appear as part of the expression $$m_1 + m_2.$$ If we switch the boxes' order, it's equivalent to switching $$m_1$$ and $$m_2$$ in the problem. However, that gives us $$m_2 + m_1$$ instead of $$m_1 + m_2$$ in the equations we found. Since these are the same thing as each other, the acceleration is unchanged by switching the order of the masses. Therefore, $$\boxed{a = 3.53 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}}.$$

The tension is almost unchanged as well. However, if we think about box $$1,$$ it's now in front of box $$2,$$ but still sliding down the incline at faster than the acceleration it would slide down alone. Therefore, it is receiving an extra push forward, not a pull forward. So the magnitude of the force from the rod is the same, but the rod is under compression, not tension. We can represent this by saying the tension is negative, $$\boxed{T = -0.940 \;\mathrm{N}}.$$

source: Robert Resnick, David Halliday, Kenneth S. Krane. Physics, Volume 1, 5th Edition (Page 115). Wiley. Kindle Edition.

problems.statement: A $$195\;\mathrm{lb}$$ man standing on a surface of negligible friction kicks forward a $$0.158 \;\mathrm{lb}$$ stone lying at his feet so that it acquires a velocity of $$12.7\;\mathrm{ft/s}$$. What velocity does the man acquire as a result?
problems.solution:
This problem is a good demonstration of the conservation of momentum. Since there is no net force acting on the system, we know that the total momentum before and after the man kicks the stone remains the same.

Before the man kicks the stone, nothing is moving, so the total momentum is just $$0$$. After the man kicks the stone, the combined momentum of the man and the stone is
$$
    (195\;\mathrm{lb})\cdot v + (0.158\;\mathrm{lb})(12.7\;\mathrm{ft/s}),
$$
where $$v$$ is the velocity of the man. These two momentums are equal, so we solve for $$v$$ to get
$$
    (195\;\mathrm{lb}) \cdot v + (0.158\;\mathrm{lb})(12.7\;\mathrm{ft/s}) = 0 \implies \boxed{v = -0.0103\;\mathrm{ft/s}}.
$$
The negative indicates that the man is moving in the opposite direction of the stone, which makes sense.

Source: HRK Ex 6.16

problems.statement: A ball of radius $$R$$ and mass $$m$$ is put inside a thin shell of the same mass and radius $$2R$$. The system is at rest on a horizontal frictionless surface initially. When the ball is released inside the shell, it sloshes around in the shell and eventually stops at the bottom of the shell. How far does the shell move from its initial contact point with the surface?
problems.solution:
The key idea in this problem is to analyze the center of mass of the system. If we define the system as the shell and the ball, then the only external forces on the system are the gravitational forces and the normal force on the shell. None of these forces are horizontal, so momentum is conserved in the horizontal direction. This also means that the horizontal velocity of the CoM is always zero (since the system initially starts at rest). As a result, the CoM's initial horizontal position is the **same** as its final horizontal position.

This is something to remember for future problems: when there are no outside forces in some particular direction, the center of mass has zero velocity in that direction. Specifically, if we choose a frame where the center of mass starts out stationary and there are no outside forces, then the center of mass doesn't move. Pieces of the system may independently move, but if some piece moves left, some other piece will move right so that the center of mass is stationary.

If we define the initial center of the shell to be $$x=0$$, we can calculate the initial CoM's $$x$$-coordinate:
$$x_\text{CoM} = \frac{m_\text{ball}\cdot x_\text{ball} + m_\text{shell}\cdot x_\text{shell}}{m_\text{ball} + m_\text{shell}} = \frac{m \cdot (-R) + m\cdot 0}{m + m} = -\frac R2.$$
Thus, the final CoM's $$x$$-coordinate will also be $$-\frac R2$$.

The final CoM and the final contact point have the the same $$x$$-coordinate, so the shell's contact point moves from $$x=0$$ to $$x=-\frac R2$$, which means the answer is $$\boxed{\frac R2}$$.

source: F=ma 2017 Problem 3

problems.statement: A ball with mass $$m$$ is projected horizontally off the end of a table with an initial kinetic energy $$K$$. At a time $$t$$ after it leaves the end of the table it has kinetic energy $$3K$$. What is $$t$$? Neglect air resistance.
problems.solution:
This problem involves a projectile, so it might be a good idea to use a kinematics approach. However, we're only provided with energies - velocities would be much more helpful in kinematics. Thus, we can try to convert our kinetic energies into velocities and then apply kinematics.

Let the original velocity of the ball be $$v_0.$$ Then, we have
$$K = \frac12 m v_0^2 \iff v_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2K}{m}}.$$

At time $$t$$, the KE has increased by a factor of 3. Since $$KE \propto v^2$$, the velocity must increase by a factor of $$\sqrt3$$, so $$v_t = v_0\sqrt3$$. This velocity has components $$v_{tx}$$ and $$v_{ty}$$. The $$x$$-component of a projectile's velocity never changes, so $$v_{tx} = v_0$$. Then, we can use the Pythagorean Theorem to calculate the $$y$$-component:
$$v_{tx}^2 + v_{ty}^2 = v_t^2 \implies v_{ty} = v_0\sqrt2.$$

Then, to calculate $$t$$, we can use the vertical acceleration of the projectile, which is $$g$$.
$$t = \frac{\Delta v_y}{a_y} = \frac{v_0\sqrt2}{g} = \sqrt{\frac{2K}{m}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt2}{g} = \boxed{\frac 2g \cdot \sqrt{\frac{K}{m}}}.$$

source: F=ma 2010 Problem 12

problems.statement: A $$2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object falls from rest a distance of $$5.0$$ meters onto a $$6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object that is supported by a vertical massless spring with spring constant $$k = 72 \;\mathrm{N/m}$$. The two objects stick together after the collision, which results in the mass/spring system oscillating. What is the maximum magnitude of the displacement of the $$6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object from its original location (its location before it is struck by the falling object)?
problems.solution:
This problem combines conservation of momentum and conservation of energy. The initial collision is inelastic, which means energy is lost, so we first have to use conservation of momentum before analyzing energy. However, after the initial collision, no more energy is lost, so we can use conservation of energy to finish the problem.

Define up as the positive direction. After falling 5 meters, the 2 kilogram object will have a velocity which can be found with 
$$v^2 = 2a\Delta y \approx 2 (10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2})(5.0 \;\mathrm{m}) = 100 \;\mathrm{m^2/s^2} \implies v = -10 \;\mathrm{m/s} .$$

By conservation of momentum, we can find the velocity of the 8.0 kg composite object after the collision:
$$v_0(8.0 \;\mathrm{kg}) = (-10 \;\mathrm{m/s})(2.0 \;\mathrm{kg}) + (0 \;\mathrm{m/s})(6.0 \;\mathrm{kg}) \implies v_0 = -2.5 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$

Now, to use conservation of energy, we must analyze kinetic energy, gravitational PE, and elastic PE:
$$\frac12 mv_0^2 + mgy_0 + \frac12 ky_0^2 = \frac12 mv_f^2 + mgy_f + \frac12 ky_f^2.$$

We already know $$v_0$$ and $$m$$. When the object is at its maximum displacement, it will be turning around, so $$v_f = 0$$. Define $$y=0$$ as the equilibrium position of the spring. We need to know $$y_0$$, the initial displacement of the spring from its equilibrium position. This displacement is caused by the weight of the 6 kilogram object:
$$ky_0 = -mg \implies y_0 = -\frac{mg}{k} = -\frac{(6.0 \;\mathrm{kg})(10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2})}{72 \;\mathrm{N/m}} \approx -0.83 \;\mathrm{m}$$
Now, we can find $$y_f$$. The initial energy is

$$\frac12 (8 \;\mathrm{kg})(-2.5 \;\mathrm{m/s})^2 + (8 \;\mathrm{kg})(10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2})(-0.83 \;\mathrm{m}) + \frac12 (72 \;\mathrm{N/m})(-0.83 \;\mathrm{m})^2 = -16.60 \;\mathrm{J}$$
so we can solve the quadratic
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac12 (8 \;\mathrm{kg})(0 \;\mathrm{m/s})^2 + (8 \;\mathrm{kg})(10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2})y_f + \frac12 (72 \;\mathrm{N/m})y_f^2 &= -16.60 \;\mathrm{J} \\
(36 \;\mathrm{J/m^2})y_f^2 + (80 \;\mathrm{J/m})y_f + (16.60 \;\mathrm{J}) &= 0,
\end{aligned}$$
which yields $$y_f = -1.99 \;\mathrm{m}$$ or $$y_f = -0.23 \;\mathrm{m}$$. Thus, the possible displacements are
$$(-1.99 \;\mathrm{m}) - (-0.83 \;\mathrm{m}) = -1.16 \;\mathrm{m}$$
or
$$(-0.23 \;\mathrm{m}) - (-0.83 \;\mathrm{m}) = 0.60\;\mathrm{m}$$

The problem asks for the __maximum__ magnitude, so the answer is $$\boxed{1.1 \;\mathrm{m}}$$.

A better answer might be $$1.2 \;\mathrm{m},$$ but that was not one of the choices on the official exam. It is best to choose the closest answer in case some small rounding error like this occurs.

source: F=ma 2015 Problem 23

problems.statement: A block with mass $$m$$ starts from rest and slides down a plane inclined at an angle $$\theta$$. The coefficient of kinetic friction is $$\mu$$. Which equation correctly yields the block's speed $$v$$ after it has traveled a distance $$d$$ down along the plane, assuming that it does indeed start sliding down? (Here $$d$$ is a distance, so it is a positive quantity.)
problems.solution:
In this problem, we use the work-energy theorem to determine the correct equation. Since the block starts at rest, and the final speed of the block is $$v$$, the change in energy is $$\frac{mv^2}{2}$$, giving us the right side of the equation we are looking for.

We know that the work done on the block is $$F \cdot d$$, where $$F$$ is the force exerted on the block.

We can compute the normal force to be $$F_N = mg \cos\theta$$, and then this means that $$F_f = \mu mg\cos\theta$$. The component of $$mg$$ that is perpendicular to the surface of the inclined plane is cancelled out by the normal force, and the remaining component is $$mg \sin\theta$$ going down the surface. This gives the total force of $$F = mg \sin\theta - \mu mg\cos\theta$$. Multiplying by $$d$$, we have the work
$$
    Fd = mgd \sin\theta - \mu mgd \cos\theta.
$$

Combining this with the change in kinetic energy, we get the answer of (b) $$\boxed{mgd \sin\theta - \mu mgd \cos\theta = \frac{mv^2}{2}}$$.

Source: Morin 5.7

problems.statement:
A small block of mass $$m$$ is moving on a horizontal table surface at initial speed $$v_0$$. It then moves smoothly onto a sloped big block of mass $$M$$. The big block can also move on the table surface. The block slides up the slope a ways, then turns around and slides back down, and moves smoothly back onto the table.

Assume that everything moves without friction. Find the speed $$v$$ of the small block after it leaves the slope and returns to the table.
problems.solution:
Let's try to work backwards and start with an easier problem. Let's suppose that the block of mass $$m$$ starts on the sloped block at a height of $$h$$.

At this point in time, there is zero kinetic energy but there is gravitational potential energy. Suppose that after the block slides down the ramp, the velocity of the block of mass $$m$$ is $$v_1$$ and the velocity of the block of mass $$M$$ is $$v_2$$. By conservation of momentum and conservation of energy, we have the following two equations:
$$\begin{aligned}
    m v_1 + M v_2 &= 0 \\
    \frac{1}{2} m v_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} M v_2^2 &= mgh
\end{aligned}$$
Solving for $$v_2$$ in the first equation and substituting into the second equation,
$$
    \frac{1}{2} m v_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} \frac{m^2}{M} v_1^2 = mgh
$$
Dividing by $$m$$ and combining the left side gives
$$
    \frac{m + M}{2M} v_1^2 = gh \implies v_1^2 = \frac{2Mgh}{m + M}.
$$

Therefore, if we find the height that the block of mass $$m$$ goes to on the sloped block, then we can find the final speed of the block after it leaves the slope. Let's think about the original problem again.

At this initial state, the momentum of the system is $$m v_0$$ in the horizontal direction, and the total energy of the system is $$\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2$$. When the square block travels up the sloped block and stops at a height of $$h$$, then they will both be moving at some velocity $$v'$$. Then the momentum of the system is $$(m + M)v'$$ and the energy is $$\frac{1}{2}(m + M)v'^2 + mgh$$. By conservation of momentum and conservation of energy, we know
$$\begin{aligned}
    m v_0 &= (m + M)v' \\
    \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 &= \frac{1}{2} (m + M) v'^2 + mgh.
\end{aligned}$$
The first equation tells us $$v' = \frac{m}{m + M} v_0$$, so substituting this into the second equation gives us
$$
    \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{m^2}{m + M} v_0^2 + mgh.
$$
Solving for $$h$$ gives us $$h = \frac{1}{2g} \frac{M}{m + M} v_0^2$$.

Now we can use the formula for $$v_1$$ we derived earlier. One thing to be careful about is that earlier, we started with the situation where both blocks are not moving, while in this case the blocks are both moving to the right with velocity $$v'$$. We can deal with this easily by changing our reference frame to one where the blocks are not moving. Since this reference frame is inertial (i.e. moving at a constant velocity), our formula from before is still valid. We also have to remember to add $$v' = \frac{m}{m + M} v_0$$ to get the answer in the original frame of reference.

We have in the new reference frame
$$
    v_1^2 = \frac{2Mgh}{m + M} = \left(\frac{M}{m + M}\right)^2 v_0^2.
$$
Since the square block is moving to the left, $$v_1$$ is negative. In particular, $$v_1 = -\frac{M}{m + M} v_0$$. To get the speed in the original reference frame, we add $$v'$$ to get
$$
    v = v_1 + v' = -\frac{M}{m + M} v_0 + \frac{m}{m + M} v_0 = \frac{m - M}{m + M} v_0.
$$
Since the problem asks for the speed of the block, we take the absolute value of this to get $$\boxed{\frac{M - m}{m + M} v_0}$$.

Source: F=ma 2010 #16

problems.statement: A bungee-jump cord has length $$\ell$$ and is initially folded back on itself, as shown in the figure. The jumper has mass $$m$$. After she jumps (or rather falls) off the platform, she is in freefall for a height $$\ell$$. After that, the spring becomes stretched. Assume that it acts like an ideal spring with a particular spring constant. (This applies only during the stretching motion, of course; the cord can't support compression like a normal spring.) It is observed that the lowest point the jumper reaches is a distance of $$2\ell$$ below the platform. What is the jumper's maximum speed?
problems.solution:
At the point where the jumper's speed is maximized, the total acceleration of the jumper is $$0$$. This means that the force is zero, i.e. $$kx = mg \implies x = \frac{mg}{k}.$$ Here, we've defined $$x$$ to be the amount the cord is stretched past its equilibrium length. To find the spring constant $$k$$, if we consider the energy at the lowest point, we know
$$
    mg(2\ell) = \frac{1}{2} k \ell^2 \implies k = \frac{4mg}{\ell}.
$$
This means $$x = \frac{\ell}{4}.$$

To find the velocity at this point, we can use the work-energy theorem. The work done on the jumper is entirely done by gravity, and this has been changed to kinetic energy and the potential energy of the spring. More specifically, we know that the jumper has fallen a distance of $$\frac{5\ell}{4}$$, and the spring has been stretched a distance of $$\frac{\ell}{4}$$, so
$$
    \frac{5}{4} mg\ell
        = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} k \left(\frac{\ell}{4}\right)^2
$$
Since $$k = \frac{4mg}{\ell},$$ this equation becomes
$$
       \dfrac54 mg \ell = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} \frac{4mg}{\ell} \frac{\ell^2}{16}.
$$
Simplifying,
$$
       \dfrac54 mg \ell = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{8} mg \ell.
$$
Solving gives $$\boxed{v = \frac{3}{2} \sqrt{g\ell}}.$$

Source: Morin, __Problems and Solutions in Introductory Mechanics__, 2014. ch 5

problems.statement: A "stiff" spring has a force law given by $$F = -kx^3$$. The work required to stretch the spring from the relaxed state $$x = 0$$ to $$x = l$$ is $$W_0$$. In terms of $$W_0$$, how much work is required to extend the spring from the stretched length $$l$$ to the length $$2l$$?
problems.solution:
We can think about the work required to stretch the spring as the area underneath the plot of force with respect to distance. By Newton's third law, the force that is stretching the string is opposite of the force that the spring exerts, and is given by $$kx^3$$. Therefore, we want to compare the following two areas

To think about how these two areas are related, let's consider the plot of $$F(x/2)$$, where we consider force to be a function of position. We get the following plot:

Let $$R$$ be the region under $$F(x/2)$$ from $$0$$ to $$2l$$. Note that $$R$$ is the same as the region under $$F(x)$$ from $$0$$ to $$l$$ stretched horizontally by a factor of $$2.$$ Therefore, the area of $$R$$ is $$2W_0.$$

We can also compare $$R$$ to the region under $$F(x)$$ from $$0$$ to $$2\ell$$. Note that
$$
    F(x/2) = -k(x/2)^3 = -\tfrac{1}{8}k x^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}F(x).
$$
Therefore, the area of $$R$$ is $$1/8$$ of the area of the region under $$F(x)$$ from $$0$$ to $$2l$$. This means that the work required to stretch the string from $$0$$ to $$2l$$ is $$16 W_0$$. Subtracting the work required to stretch the spring from $$0$$ to $$l$$, we have the answer of $$\boxed{15 W_0}$$.

Source: Halliday, Resnick, Krane __Physics__, 5th ed. 2002. Problem 11.13

problems.statement:
A stone of weight $$w$$ is launched vertically upward into the air from ground height. Its initial speed is $$v_0$$. Suppose that the air drag force $$f$$ dissipates an amount $$fy$$ of mechanical energy as the stone travels a distance $$y$$.

What is the maximum height reached by the stone?
problems.solution:
Consider the change of the stone's kinetic energy from when it is initially thrown to when it reaches its maximum height. Since the stone initially has speed $$v_0$$ and at the maximum height it has speed $$0$$, the change in kinetic energy is $$-\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 = -\frac{1}{2} \frac{w}{g} v_0^2$$, where $$m = \frac{w}{g}$$ is the mass of the stone.

By the work-energy theorem, this is equal to the work done on the stone. From gravity, the work done is $$-mgh = -wh$$. From air resistance, the work done is $$-fh$$. Therefore,
$$
    -\frac{1}{2} \frac{w}{g} v_0^2 = -wh - fh = -(w + f)h.
$$
Solving for $$h$$ gives
$$
    h = \frac{w}{2g(w + f)} v_0^2 = \boxed{\frac{v_0^2}{2g(1 + f/w)}}.
$$

Source: HKR Problem 13.1

problems.statement:
A stone of weight $$w$$ is launched vertically upward into the air from ground height. Its initial speed is $$v_0$$. Suppose that the air drag force $$f$$ dissipates an amount $$fy$$ of mechanical energy as the stone travels a distance $$y$$.

What is the speed of the stone upon impact with the ground?
problems.solution:
Since the stone travels a distance of $$h$$ while going up and $$h$$ while coming back down, the total energy lost is $$2fh$$. Therefore, the final kinetic energy after coming back down can be written as
$$
    \frac{1}{2} \frac{w}{g} v^2 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{w}{g} v_0^2 - 2fh.
$$
Substituting in the value for $$h$$ from part (a),
$$
    \frac{1}{2} \frac{w}{g} v^2 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{w}{g} v_0^2 - \frac{2f v_0^2}{2g(1 + f/w)}.
$$
Multiplying by $$2g/w$$ and rearranging,
$$\begin{aligned}
    v^2 &= v_0^2 - \frac{2f v_0^2}{w(1 + f/w)} \\
        &= \frac{(w + f) v_0^2- 2f v_0^2}{(w+f)} \\
        &= \frac{(w - f) v_0^2}{(w + f)}.
\end{aligned}$$
Therefore,
$$
    v = \boxed{v_0\left(\frac{w - f}{w + f}\right)^{1/2}}.
$$

problems.statement:
In this week's USAPhO-style problem, we will examine the basic physics behind the flight of a bird. Imagine an bird viewed from the frame where the bird is stationary and wind rushes past the bird at speed $$v.$$ (For convenience, we ignore the flapping of the birds wings and think of them as fixed, with an ability to push air past them.)

The density of the air is $$\rho.$$ The bird has wings of length $$l$$ (direction of its wingspan) and depth $$d.$$ (The thickness of the bird's wings is not considered in this model.)

**a)** Suppose the wings are angled at some angle $$\theta$$ with respect to the incoming wind. The wings interact with all the air that is on a direct collision course with some part of the wing. Below, the incoming air is blue and the tilted wing is black. The length $$l$$ of the wing is into and out of your monitor.

How much air (in mass of air per unit time) do the wings interact with, as a function of $$v, \rho, l, d,$$ and $$\theta?$$

**b)** Suppose that as air flows past the wing, it is deflected downward by an angle $$\theta$$ while keeping constant speed. Find the weight $$W$$ of the bird in terms of $$v, \rho, l, d,$$ and $$\theta.$$

**c)** Suppose two birds have the same shape, but bird $$B$$ is twice the size of bird $$A$$ in every dimension. Assuming $$\theta$$ is the same for both birds, if bird $$A$$ flies at speed $$v,$$ what speed must bird $$B$$ fly?

**d)** The upward force from the air to the bird is called the **lift**. There is also a backwards force on the bird, called the **drag**. Generally, birds can be considered to have a fixed ratio of lift force magnitude to drag force magnitude. Call this ratio $$\alpha.$$ Find the power bird must provide as a function of $$v, \rho, l, d, \theta,$$ and $$\alpha.$$

**e)** Some data on the weight $$(W),$$ given in Newtons, and wing area $$(S),$$ given in square meters, and flying speed of various birds is provided in the chart below. Make a plot of the data on this chart showing how well the theory outlined in part (b) matches the real-world data. Your plot should be set up so that if the model is perfectly accurate, you will see a straight line on the plot.

__data source: Tennekes, Hendrik. The simple science of flight: from insects to jumbo jets. MIT press, 2009.__
problems.solution:
**a)** We examine how much air is crossing the red line shown below per unit time.

The red line has height $$d\sin\theta$$ and runs into and out of the page a distance $$l.$$ So its area is $$dl\sin\theta.$$ In a time $$t,$$ the volume of air that rushes past the red line is its area times $$vt,$$ so the volume of air that the wing interacts with per unit time is $$\dfrac{vt\cdot dl\sin\theta}{t} = vdl\sin\theta.$$

The mass of this air is found by multiplying by the density, $$\boxed{\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t} = \rho v d l \sin\theta}.$$

**b)** We look at the momentum per unit time picked up by the air. The $$y$$-momentum of a mass $$m$$ of air moving downward at an angle $$\theta$$ is $$mv\sin\theta.$$ To find the $$y$$ momentum given to the air per unit time, we use the mass flow equation from part (a), giving $$\dfrac{\Delta p_{\mathrm{air}}}{\Delta t} = \rho v d l \sin\theta \cdot v \sin\theta = \boxed{\rho v^2 d l \sin^2\theta}.$$

This is in fact the solution to the problem. The momentum per unit time, in the $$y$$ direction, given to the air is another name for the force that the bird exerts on the air. By Newton's third law, the air exerts an equal and opposite force back on the bird. And because the bird is not accelerating up or down, that force must be equal to the bird's weight. So the boxed expression is equal to the weight of the bird.

**c)** The larger bird is twice as big in three dimensions, so it weighs $$8$$ times as much. So the quantity $$\rho v^2 d l \sin^2\theta$$ must be $$8$$ times as large for the second bird. $$\rho$$ and $$\sin\theta$$ are the same between the two birds. $$dl$$ is four times as large for the second bird as for the first, meaning $$v^2$$ must be twice as large for the second bird. This means the second bird flies at speed $$\boxed{\sqrt{2}v}.$$

**d)** In the frame of the wind, the bird is moving forward at speed $$v$$ and feels a drag force $$f_d.$$ Then the power the bird delivers to the wind is $$P = vf_d.$$ We are told $$f_d = L/\alpha = W/\alpha,$$ where $$L$$ is the lift and $$W$$ the weight of the bird. Based on part (b), we have $$P = v\cdot \dfrac{1}{\alpha} \rho v^2 d l \sin^2\theta.$$ Simplifying, we get $$\boxed{P = \dfrac{\rho v^3 d l \sin^2\theta}{\alpha}}.$$

**e)** The wing area is $$S = dl,$$ so our result from part (b) says $$W = \rho v^2 S \sin^2\theta $$ We can rewrite this as $$v^2 = \dfrac{1}{\rho \sin^2\theta} \dfrac{W}{S} .$$ If we plot $$v^2$$ on the vertical axis and $$W/S$$ on the horizontal axis, our theory predicts a straight line with a slope of $$m = \dfrac{1}{\rho \sin^2\theta}.$$

The quantity $$W/S$$ can be called the **wing loading**. It is essentially the pressure (force per unit area) on the wings.

Here is a computer-generated version of a plot of $$v^2$$ versus wing loading:

As we can see, it is very-well approximated by a straight line, verifying our model.

problems.statement: A baseball is dropped on top of a basketball. The basketball hits the ground, rebounds with a speed of $$4.0\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ and collides with the baseball as it is moving downward at $$4.0\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ After the collision, the baseball moves upward as shown in the figure and the basketball is instantaneously at rest right after the collision. The mass of the baseball is $$0.2\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and the mass of the basketball is $$0.5\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Ignore air resistance and ignore any changes in velocities due to gravity during the very short collision times. What is the speed of the baseball right after colliding with the upward moving basketball?
problems.solution:
In this problem, we have two balls colliding and changing velocities. The best way to deal with scenarios like this is with conservation of momentum.

Right before the collision, the momentum of the basketball is $$(0.5\;\mathrm{kg})(4.0 \;\mathrm{m/s})$$ and the momentum of the baseball is $$(0.2\;\mathrm{kg})(-4.0 \;\mathrm{m/s}).$$ If the velocity of the baseball right after the collision is $$v,$$ then the momentum of the basketball is $$0$$ and the momentum of the baseball is $$(0.2\;\mathrm{kg})v.$$ Therefore, by conservation of momentum,
$$
    (0.5\;\mathrm{kg})(4.0 \;\mathrm{m/s}) + (0.2\;\mathrm{kg})(-4.0 \;\mathrm{m/s}) = 0 + (0.2\;\mathrm{kg})v
    \implies v = \boxed{6.0 \;\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$

Source: F=ma 2007 #16

problems.statement: A barge with mass $$1.50\times 10^5 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ (green in the figure below) is proceeding downriver at $$6.20 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in heavy fog when it collides broadside with a barge heading directly across the river (blue in the figure). The second barge has mass $$2.78\times 10^5 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ and was moving at $$4.30 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Immediately after impact, the second barge finds its course deflected by $$18.0^\circ$$ in the downriver direction and its speed increased to $$5.10\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ The river current was practically zero at the time of the accident. What is the speed and direction of motion of the first barge immediately after the collision?
problems.solution:
This is a standard problem with masses colliding resulting in changing momenta. The key idea is that the momentum in each component is conserved.

In the horizontal direction (corresponding to the diagram), conservation of momentum gives
$$
    (1.50 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{kg})(6.20 \;\mathrm{m/s}) = 
    (1.50 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{kg})v_x +
    (2.78 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{kg})(5.10 \;\mathrm{m/s}) \sin 18^\circ
    \implies v_x \approx 3.28 \;\mathrm{m/s}.
$$
In the vertical direction, conservation of momentum gives
$$
    (2.78 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{kg})(4.30 \;\mathrm{m/s}) = 
    (1.50 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{kg})v_y +
    (2.78 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{kg})(5.10 \;\mathrm{m/s}) \cos 18^\circ
    \implies v_y \approx -1.02 \;\mathrm{m/s}.
$$

Therefore, the speed of motion is $$\sqrt{(3.28 \;\mathrm{m/s})^2 + (-1.02 \;\mathrm{m/s})^2} \approx \boxed{3.43 \;\mathrm{m/s}},$$ and since $$\arctan(-1.02/3.28) \approx -17.28^\circ,$$ the direction of motion is $$\boxed{17.28^\circ \text{ clockwise of downstream}}.$$

Source: HRK Exercise 6.27

problems.statement: A $$0.650\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball moving at $$5.00\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ collides with a $$0.750\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball that is originally at rest. After the collision, the $$0.750\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball moves off with a speed of $$4.00\;\mathrm{m/s}$$, and the $$0.650\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball moves off at a right angle to the final direction of motion of the $$0.750\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball. What is the final speed of the $$0.650\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball?
problems.solution:
In this problem, we are given velocities and there is a collision, so we can try to use conservation of momentum. Let's suppose that the $$0.650\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball approaches from the left, like so:

Before the collision occurs, the momentum of the system is $$(0.65\;\mathrm{kg})(5.00\;\mathrm{m/s}).$$ After the collision, suppose that we have the following momentum vectors:

Note that since the final velocities are perpendicular, adding them geometrically and using conservation of momentum will result in the following diagram, where $$p_1$$ and $$p_2$$ are the two final momentums:

Therefore, by the Pythagorean theorem, we know
$$
    [(0.65\;\mathrm{kg})(5.00\;\mathrm{m/s})]^2
    = [(0.65\;\mathrm{kg})v]^2
    + [(0.75\;\mathrm{kg})(4.00\;\mathrm{m/s})]^2
    \implies v = \boxed{1.92\;\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$

Source: F=ma 2015 #9

problems.statement:
A $$0.650\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball moving at $$5.00\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ collides with a $$0.750\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball that is originally at rest. After the collision, the $$0.750\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball moves off with a speed of $$4.00\;\mathrm{m/s}$$, and the $$0.650\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball moves off at a right angle to the final direction of motion of the $$0.750\;\mathrm{kg}$$ ball.

Let the change in total kinetic energy in this collision be defined by $$\Delta K = K_f - K_i$$, where $$K_f$$ is the total final kinetic energy, and $$K_i$$ is the total initial kinetic energy. Which of the following is true?
problems.solution:
In this problem, we are analyzing the kinetic energy of this system at different times. Since there are no external forces, we know that the kinetic energy must not increase, so $$\Delta K \leq 0$$. Since the kinetic energy of the system is positive, we have $$K_i, K_f > 0$$. This eliminates the first three answer choices.

We have $$\Delta K = K_f - K_i > -K_i$$ is always true, so in order to determine whether the answer is (d) or (e), we have to compute whether $$\Delta K$$ is zero or not. We have
$$\begin{aligned}
    K_i &= \frac{1}{2}(0.650 \;\mathrm{kg})(5.00 \;\mathrm{m/s})^2 = 8.125 \;\mathrm{J} \\
    K_f &= \frac{1}{2}(0.650 \;\mathrm{kg})(1.92 \;\mathrm{m/s})^2 + \frac{1}{2}(0.750 \;\mathrm{kg})(4.00 \;\mathrm{m/s})^2 \approx 7.20 \;\mathrm{J}.
\end{aligned}$$
Therefore, $$\Delta K \neq 0$$, and we have $$\boxed{-K_i < \Delta K < 0}$$.

problems.statement: A stream of water impinges on a stationary "dished" turbine blade, as shown in the figure. The speed of the water is $$v$$, both before and after it strikes the curved surface of the blade, and the mass of the water striking the blade per unit time is constant at the value $$\mu$$. Find the force exerted by the water on the blade.
problems.solution:
Note that by Newton's Third law, it is equivalent to find the force exerted by the blade on the water. Since this problem involves masses with changing velocities, it makes sense to try to use momentum. Working with mass per time is a bit unintuitive, so we will consider what happens over some period of time $$t$$.

We have an amount of water with mass $$\mu t$$ and velocity $$\vec v$$ hit the blade. This water has momentum $$\mu t \vec v$$. After striking the blade, the water has momentum $$-\mu t \vec v$$. Therefore, the impulse that the blade exerted on the water is the difference of these, i.e. $$-2\mu t \vec v$$. Since impulse is the product of force and time, the force exerted by the blade on the water is $$-2\mu \vec v$$. Therefore the force exerted by the water on the blade is $$\boxed{2\mu \vec v}$$.

Source: HRK 6.1

problems.statement: A ball with mass $$m$$ moves in the positive $$x$$ direction with speed $$v$$, as shown in the figure. It collides elastically with two other balls (also with mass $$m$$) which are situated so that they both move at equal speeds at equal angles of $$45^\circ$$ with respect to the $$x$$-axis after the collision. If the first ball has final speed $$v_1$$ and the other two balls have final speed $$v_2$$, what are $$v_1$$ and $$v_2$$?
problems.solution:
In this problem, we're given an elastic collision, so we know that both momentum and energy are conserved. Conservation of momentum gives
$$
    v_1 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} v_2 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} v_2 = v
    \implies v_1 + \sqrt 2 v_2 = v,
$$
and conservation of energy gives
$$
    2\left(\frac{1}{2} m v_2^2\right) + \frac{1}{2} m v_1^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v^2
    \implies 2 v_2^2 + v_1^2 = v^2.
$$
Substituting in $$2 v_2^2 = (\sqrt 2 v_2)^2 = (v - v_1)^2$$ from conservation of momentum,
$$
    (v - v_1)^2 + v_1^2 = v^2 \implies 2v_1^2 - 2v v_1 = 0 \implies v_1 = 0 \text{ or } v_1 = v.
$$
These correspond to $$v_2 = v/\sqrt{2} \text{ or } 0$$ respectively. Since $$v_2 > 0$$, we have $$\boxed{(v_1, v_2) = (0, v/\sqrt 2)}$$. It is interesting to note that the solution $$(v, 0)$$ that we discarded corresponds to the situation where the balls do not actually collide.

Source: Morin Problem 6.17

problems.statement: A stream of $$10$$ clay balls with mass $$m$$ move with speed $$v$$ in a line across a frictionless table. The spacing between them is $$\ell$$. An additional ball with mass $$m$$ sits at rest in front of them, as shown in the figure. The front moving ball collides with the stationary ball and sticks to it and forms a blob of mass $$2m$$. Then the second ball collides with the blob and forms a blob of mass $$3m$$. And so on. How much time elapses between the instant shown below (when all the balls are separated by $$\ell$$) and the last collision?
problems.solution:
Here, we have $$10$$ balls moving at the same velocity. It would be easier if we were to work in the frame where those balls are all initially at rest. In this frame, we have the following initial setup:

It takes $$\ell/v$$ time for the rightmost ball to collide with the next ball. By conservation of momentum, the new speed of the blob is
$$
    mv + m\cdot 0 = 2m v_f \implies v_f = v/2.
$$

Then, it takes $$2\ell/v$$ time for the blob of mass $$2m$$ to collide with the next ball. By conservation of momentum again, the new speed of the blob is
$$
    (2m)(v/2) + m\cdot 0 = 3m v_f \implies v_f = v/3.
$$

In general, we will have that the blob will take $$n\ell/v$$ time for the $$n$$th collision. This gives a total time of
$$
    (1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + 10) \ell/v = \boxed{55\ell/v}.
$$

Source: Morin Problem 6.12

problems.statement: A flat car of mass $$m_0$$ starts moving to the right due to a constant horizontal force $$F$$. Sand spills on the flat car from a stationary hopper. The velocity of the loading is constant and is equal to $$\mu$$, with units $$\mathrm{kg/s}$$. What is the velocity of the car in the process of loading as a function of time?
problems.solution:
This problem involves different masses and changing velocities, so it's probably a good idea to think about the momentum. We know that at time $$t$$, the mass of the car is $$m_0 + \mu t$$, and the impulse exerted on the car is $$Ft$$. Then we have
$$
    p = Ft  = mv = (m_0 + \mu t) v \implies v = \boxed{\frac{Ft}{m_0 + \mu t}}.
$$

Source: Irodov 1.183

problems.statement: A flat car of mass $$m_0$$ starts moving to the right due to a constant horizontal force $$F$$. Sand spills on the flat car from a stationary hopper. The velocity of the loading is constant and is equal to $$\mu$$, with units $$\mathrm{kg/s}$$. What is the acceleration of the car in the process of loading as a function of time?
problems.solution:
It is tempting to think that $$F = ma = (m_0 + \mu t) a,$$ which will mean that $$a = \frac{F}{m_0 + \mu t},$$ but that is not quite correct because $$F$$ is not the only force on the car. When the sand falls onto the car, it is not moving at the same velocity as the car, so the car must exert a force on the sand in order to accelerate it to the same velocity as the car. By Newton's third law, the sand must exert a force onto the car as well.

To calculate this force, note that force is equal to the change of momentum of the sand per unit time. Since we are accelerating $$\mu$$ sand per unit time to a velocity of $$v$$, we know that $$\mu v$$ is precisely the force that the car exerts on the sand. By Newton's third law, we know that the sand exerts $$-\mu v$$ force onto the car.

Therefore, the net force on the car is $$F - \mu v,$$ and we can now write
$$
  F - \mu v = ma = (m_0 + \mu t) a
$$
From part a, we have $$v = \frac{Ft}{m_0 + \mu t},$$ so
$$
  F - \frac{F \mu t}{m_0 + \mu t} = (m_0 + \mu t) a
  \implies \boxed{a = \frac{F m_0}{(m_0 + \mu t)^2}}.
$$

Source: Irodov 1.143

problems.statement:
A shell flying with speed $$v = 500 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ bursts into three identical fragments. As it does, the kinetic energy of the system increases by $$50\%.$$

What is the fastest possible speed of any one of the fragments after the shell bursts?
problems.solution:
Although kinetic energies change with a change of reference frames, potential energies, such as the energy stored in whatever mechanism causes the shell to burst, do not. Therefore the change in kinetic energy of the fragments is the same in all frames. We can call this change $$\Delta T.$$

We will work in the frame of the shell and maximize the speed of a single fragment, then go back to the original frame.

Call the fastest fragment fragment 1 and the others fragments 2 and 3.  Call the direction of motion of fragment 1 the right. Then the center of mass of fragments 2 and 3 taken together moves left because, by conservation of momentum, the center of mass of the system of all three fragments is stationary in the shell frame.

Suppose fragments 2 and 3 individually had some motion outside of the left/right direction. For example, fragment 2 had some upward motion and fragment 3 had some downward motion.

Imagine taking $$v_2$$ and $$v_3$$ and replacing them with their projections onto the direction of $$v_1.$$ This arrangement still conserves momentum, but we have some extra energy left over. We can use that energy to increase the velocities, and we see $$v_1$$ was not a maximum. If we get the maximum speed, all the velocities must be collinear.

We can also show that $$v_2 = v_3.$$

Suppose that $$v_3 > v_2.$$

Set $$\dfrac{v_2 + v_3}{2} = \bar{v}$$ and $$\dfrac{v_3 - v_2}{2} = \Delta v.$$ Then $$v_3 = \bar{v} + \Delta v$$ and $$v_2 = \bar{v} - \Delta v.$$

The kinetic energy is $$\dfrac12 \dfrac{m}{3} \left(\bar{v} + \Delta v\right)^2 + \dfrac12 \dfrac{m}{3} \left(\bar{v} - \Delta v\right)^2 = \dfrac{m}{3} \left( \bar{v}^2 + (\Delta v)^2\right).$$

If we set $$\Delta v = 0,$$ we don't affect the total momentum of the leftward-moving fragments, but we reduce their kinetic energy, again leaving more energy to increase the velocities. Therefore, when $$v_1$$ is maximized, $$v_2 = v_3.$$

By conservation of momentum, we have
$$ v_1 + v_2 + v_3 = 0.$$

By conservation of energy, we have
$$ \dfrac12 \dfrac{m}{3} v_1^2 + \dfrac12\dfrac{m}{3} v_2^2 + \dfrac12 \dfrac{m}{3}v_3^2 = \Delta T.$$

Along with $$v_2 = v_3,$$ this shows, after simplification $$v_1^2 = \dfrac{4}{m} \Delta T.$$

The original question implies $$\Delta T = 0.5 \dfrac12 mv^2,$$ and so, after simplification, $$v_1 = v.$$

That means fragment 1 moves at $$500 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in the shell frame.

The fastest possible speed in the original frame is if fragment 1 moves in the same direction in the shell frame that the shell moves in the original frame, so the fastest possible speed is $$500 \;\mathrm{m/s} + 500 \;\mathrm{m/s} = 1000 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

Source: Irodov 1.208

problems.statement: A block of wood with a mass of $$M = 2.5 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ is suspended from fixed pegs by vertical strings $$l = 3.0 \;\mathrm{m},$$ in a set up known as a ballistic pendulum. A bullet with a mass of $$m = 10 \;\mathrm{g}$$ and moving horizontally with a velocity $$v = 300 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ enters and remains in the block. Find the maximum angle $$\theta$$ to the vertical through which the block swings.
problems.solution:
There are two parts to this problem. First, we have to deal with the collision between the bullet and the block. Then, we deal with the block rising after the collision. The collision is an inelastic one, so we can use conservation of momentum. Then, as the block rises, it conserves energy. So each of these principles applies to this problem, but in different places.

Before the collision, the system has momentum $$mv,$$ and this momentum is conserved during the collision. If the speed of the block+bullet together after the collision is $$V,$$ then momentum conservation says $$mv = (M+m)V.$$

The kinetic energy of the block+bullet after the collision is $$\dfrac12 (M+m)V^2,$$ and so by energy conservation, $$\dfrac12 (M+m)V^2 = (M+m)gh,$$ where $$h$$ is the height to which the block and bullet rise. Using substitution, we can write $$h = \dfrac{V^2}{2g} = \dfrac{m^2v^2}{2(M+m)^2g} $$

The question asks for the angle $$\theta$$ that the block rises from the vertical. To find this, we note $$h = l(1 - \cos\theta).$$ Substituting and solving for $$\theta,$$ we obtain $$\theta = \mathrm{arccos}\left(1 - \dfrac{m^2v^2}{2(M+m)^2 gl}\right).$$

Plugging in the numbers given in the problem, we finally get 
$$\theta = 12.5^\circ.$$

To within the accuracy given by the solution choices, that's choice **(b)**, or $$\boxed{13^\circ}.$$

problems.statement:
This problem investigates **Compton scattering**, which is when a particle of light collides with a charged particle, usually an electron. During this process, the light particle gives some of its energy to the electron. This means the photon's energy goes down, which in turn means its wavelength gets longer. The explanation of Compton scattering (by Arthur Compton) in 1923 gave additional credence to the then-young idea that light consists of particles, which we know today as photons.

This is a type of 2D, elastic collision. In this collision, both momentum and energy are conserved. However, the formulas for momentum and energy are those used in special relativity and quantum mechanics, so not everything we've learned about collisions applies to Compton scattering.

A photon does not have mass, but it does have energy and momentum. Its energy is 
$$E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}.$$
Here, $$h$$ is a constant known as **Planck's constant**, which is used ubiquitously in quantum mechanics. $$c$$ is the speed of light, and $$\lambda$$ is the wavelength of the photon.

The magnitude of the momentum of a photon is
$$p = \dfrac{E}{c}.$$

An electron does have mass, which we will call $$m.$$ The equations of special relativity tell us that the momentum and energy of an electron moving with velocity $$\mathbf{v}$$ are

$$\mathbf{p} = \dfrac{m\mathbf{v}}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$$

and

$$E =\sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2 c^4}$$

We will consider a stationary electron and a photon which approaches from the left. The photon and electron collides, and the photon winds up traveling away up and to the right, at an angle $$\theta$$ with its previous trajectory. The photon's wavelength after the collision has increased to $$\lambda',$$ and the electron moves down and to the right.

__By JabberWok, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=2078004__

**a)** Find an equation for energy conservation in the scattering process described above. You may need to introduce new variables for the speed and angle between the electron's final direction of motion and the original direction of motion of the photon.

**b)** Find an equation for momentum conservation in the original direction of travel of the photon.

**c)** Find an equation for momentum conservation in the direction perpendicular to the direction of travel of the photon.

**d)** Define $$\lambda_c = \dfrac{h}{mc}.$$ This is called the **Compton wavelength** of the electron. Also define $$\lambda_e$$ so that $$p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda_e}$$ for an electron. Rewrite the above formulas using these definitions. Eliminate $$h, c, v, m$$ and any variables other than the angles and the various $$\lambda's (\lambda, \lambda', \lambda_e, \lambda_c)$$ from your equations.

**e)** Eliminate the variable you introduced for the angle of motion of the electron. You may need to use the fact that $$\cos^2x + \sin^2 x = 1.$$ Solve the remaining equations to find $$\lambda' - \lambda,$$ the change in wavelength of the photon as a function of $$\lambda_c$$ and $$\theta.$$
problems.solution:
**a)** The equation is $$\boxed{\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} + mc^2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda'} + \sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2c^4}}.$$

**b)** The equation is $$\boxed{\dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda'}\cos\theta + \dfrac{mv'\cos\phi}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{v'^2}{c^2}}}}$$
where $$v'$$ is the speed of the electron after the collision and $$\phi$$ is the angle the electron's path makes with the horizontal after the collision.

**c)** The equation is $$\boxed{0 = \dfrac{h}{\lambda'}\sin\theta + \dfrac{mv'\sin\phi}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{v'^2}{c^2}}}}.$$

**d)** The definition of $$\lambda_c$$ implies $$mc = \dfrac{h}{\lambda_c}.$$ Making the substitutions, the equation from (a) becomes
$$\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} + \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_c} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda'} + \sqrt{\dfrac{h^2c^2}{\lambda_e^2} + \dfrac{h^2c^2}{\lambda_c^2}}.$$

This simplifies to 
$$\boxed{\dfrac{1}{\lambda} + \dfrac{1}{\lambda_c} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda'} + \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{\lambda_e^2} + \dfrac{1}{\lambda_c^2}}}.$$

Making substitutions into the equation from part (b) and canceling the common factor $$h$$ in the numerators, we find

$$\boxed{\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\lambda'} + \dfrac{\cos\phi}{\lambda_e}}.$$

Making the same substitutions and simplifications to the equation from part (c), we get

$$\boxed{0 = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\lambda'} + \dfrac{\sin\phi}{\lambda_e}}.$$

**e)** We introduced the variable $$\phi.$$ To eliminate it, we'll use both of the momentum conservation equations. Solving the equation for the perpendicular direction for $$\sin\phi,$$ we get 
$$\sin\phi = -\dfrac{\lambda_e \sin\theta}{\lambda'}.$$
Solving the other momentum equation for $$\cos\phi,$$ we get
$$\cos\phi = \lambda_e\left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} - \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\lambda'}\right).$$

Adding the squares of these two equations and using $$\cos^2x + \sin^2x = 1,$$ we get
$$ \dfrac{\lambda_e^2 \sin^2\theta}{\lambda'^2} + \lambda_e^2\left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} - \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\lambda'}\right)^2 = 1.$$

Expanding the squared term with parentheses will give us a $$\cos^2\theta$$ term which can be added to the $$\sin^2\theta$$ term. Doing this and dividing by $$\lambda_e^2,$$ we get

$$\dfrac{1}{\lambda'^2} + \left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} - \dfrac{2\cos\theta}{\lambda'\lambda}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\lambda_e^2}.$$

Next, we need to use the energy conservation equation. Subtracting $$\dfrac{1}{\lambda'}$$ from each side and squaring, then subtracting $$\dfrac{1}{\lambda_c^2}$$ from each side, we get
$$\dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} + \dfrac{1}{\lambda'^2} + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda \lambda_c} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda \lambda'} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_c\lambda'}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\lambda_e^2} .$$

We can now equate the two expressions that are equal to $$\dfrac{1}{\lambda_e^2}.$$ Subtracting like terms from each side and multiplying everything by $$\dfrac12 \lambda\lambda'\lambda_c,$$ we get
$$\lambda' - \lambda_c  - \lambda = -\cos\theta \lambda_c.$$

Solving for $$\lambda' - \lambda,$$ we have
$$\boxed{\lambda' - \lambda = \lambda_c(1 - \cos\theta)}.$$

problems.statement:
Albert Einstein, after formulating his general theory of relativity, used it to predict that light traveling from a distant star and brushing past the surface of the sun should be deflected by  $$\theta = 1.8''$$ by the sun's gravity. (That's 1.8 arcseconds. One arcsecond is one 60th of an arcminute, which is one 60th of a degree.) Newtonian gravity predicted a deflection of $$0.9''.$$

Arthur Eddington and collaborators measured the deflection of starlight by the sun during the 1919 total solar eclipse. They found that light was deflected by
$$ \theta = 2'' \pm 0.3 ''.$$
Eddington claimed this confirmed general relativity over Newtonian gravity. However, many scientists were not convinced by this test. Which of the following is a valid reason to object to the conclusion that the test supports general relativity over Newtonian physics?

choices.A: The error bars on Eddington's measurement are too large; scientific evidence should be more precise than to have a $$15\%$$ error.
choices.B: Eddington may have underestimated the size of his error bars a moderate amount (a factor of 1.5 or less).
choices.C: Eddington may have underestimated the size of his error bars by a large amount (a factor of 3 or more).
choices.D: Multiple data points are needed; a single data point cannot be considered scientific evidence.
choices.E: Einstein's theory was still too new to be considered established.

problems.solution:
A measurement with large error bars can be consistent with many different theories. For example, if Eddington had reported his measurement as $$\theta = 2'' \pm 1.5'',$$ then both the $$0.9''$$ of Newtonian gravity and the $$1.8''$$ of general relativity would be well within the region of possible true values of the reflection. The measurement could therefore be consistent with either theory and would not be sufficient to distinguish between them. Answer (c) is correct - if Eddington reported error bars much too small, the correct error bars could encompass the Newtonian prediction. In fact, many scientists did claim that Eddington's error bars were too small, and that he could not make a measurement as precise as the one he claimed.

There are no scientific rules that error bars must be some minimum size, so (a) is incorrect.

(b) is incorrect because if Eddington's error bars had been somewhat larger, his result might have been, for example, $$\theta = 2'' \pm 0.45'',$$ and this would still exclude the Newtonian prediction.

While in science, it is better to have multiple data points than to have one data point, a single data point is still valid scientific evidence. (d) is incorrect.

Finally, there is no rule in science that theories be around for a certain duration before they are taken seriously, so (e) is also incorrect. (It is probably the case that when very new results are announced, scientists will be skeptical of them for a short while, but this is because they want experts in the area to have a chance to review the results carefully before accepting them, not because there is an inherent time limit involved.)

problems.statement:
You weigh 100 samples with a scale. The mean reading is $$126.1 \;\mathrm{g},$$ and the standard deviation of the readings is $$5.1 \;\mathrm{g}.$$

Although the scale you are using reports weights to the nearest tenth of a gram, you suspect that the scale is poorly-calibrated so that its readings are consistently incorrect - either all too large or all too small by the same percentage. You don't know the size of this effect, but suspect it to be on the order of $$0.5\%.$$ What is your uncertainty in the combined weight of the samples?
problems.solution:
The key to this problem is to note that the errors in the weights are not independent. If the first sample's weight is too heavy, the second, third, etc. samples' weights are also too heavy, and if the first sample's weight is too light, the remaining samples' weights are also too light. Therefore, it is not appropriate to add error in quadrature like we would if the errors were random and independent.

Instead, the scale's uncertainty is about $$0.5\%,$$ so we should report an error of about $$0.5\%.$$ Since the total weight is about $$1.26 \times 10^4 \;\mathrm{g},$$ the error is about $$0.005 \times 1.26 \times 10^4 \;\mathrm{g} = 60 \;\mathrm{g}.$$

Also, note that the extra information about the standard deviation of the weights is not relevant; this standard deviation is not the error in the scale's reading, but the innate spread in the weights of the samples. If some samples are heavier and others lighter than the mean, that doesn't affect our estimate of the mass of all of them combined.

problems.statement: Adult platypuses weigh $$2.1 \pm 0.9 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ You wish to estimate the weight of a pile of exactly 3000 adult platypuses, randomly and independently selected from the adult population. Compared to the weight of a single platypus, your estimate will have:

choices.A: larger absolute uncertainty and larger relative uncertainty
choices.B: larger absolute uncertainty and the same relative uncertainty
choices.C: larger absolute uncertainty and smaller relative uncertainty
choices.D: the same absolute uncertainty and the same relative uncertainty
choices.E: the same absolute uncertainty and smaller relative uncertainty

problems.solution:
We can apply the "one over root $$n$$" rule to this problem. The rule states that if we make $$n$$ independent measurements of a quantity each with the same uncertainty $$\sigma,$$ our final uncertainty in the quantity is $$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sigma.$$

In this case, the weight of the pile of 3000 platypuses can be considered the result of 3000 independent measurements, each with a mean of $$\mu = 2.1 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ and uncertainty $$\sigma = 0.9 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ The final uncertainty in the per-platypus weight is $$\dfrac{0.9 \;\mathrm{kg}}{\sqrt{3000}} \approx 0.016 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ In other words, on average, a platypus on the pile weighs $$2.1 \pm 0.016 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ (We should ideally report another digit on the end of the weight of an average platypus, e.g. $$2.12 \;\mathrm{kg},$$ but this data is not available.)

The total weight of the pile is therefore $$3000(2.1 \pm 0.016 \;\mathrm{kg}) = 6.3 \times 10^3 \pm 48 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

The absolute uncertainty has increased from $$0.9 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ to $$48 \;\mathrm{kg},$$ a factor of $$\sqrt{3000}.$$ However, the relative uncertainty has decreased by a factor of $$\sqrt{3000}.$$ The answer is (c).

problems.statement:
For small angles $$\theta,$$ the torque $$\tau$$ on a single pendulum of mass $$m$$ and length $$\ell$$ is 
$$\tau = \ell mg\sin\theta\,.$$

Measuring $$\theta$$ in radians, an approximation is
$$\tau \approx \ell mg \theta\,.$$

What is the approximate range of angles for which the error in this approximation for the torque value is smaller than $$1\%?$$

For this question, use the following information:

For small angles, $$\sin\theta \approx \theta,$$ where $$\theta$$ is measured in radians. (The answers are listed in degrees, so you may have to convert.)

A more-accurate equation, still using radians, is
$$\sin\theta \approx \theta - \dfrac{\theta^3}{6}\,.$$
problems.solution:
This question asks about the relative error in $$\theta$$ as an approximation for $$\sin\theta.$$

The absolute error is given to be approximately $$\dfrac{\theta^3}{6},$$ so the relative error is approximately $$\dfrac{\theta^3/6}{\theta} = \dfrac{\theta^2}{6}.$$

We would like this relative error to be smaller than about $$1\%,$$ so $$\dfrac{\theta^2}{6} < 0.01.$$

Solving, $$|\theta| < 0.24.$$ Converting from radians to degrees, we get $$|\theta|<14^\circ.$$

problems.statement:
A car competes in a race. The car begins the race with initial speed $$v_0$$ and maintains a constant acceleration $$a$$ throughout the race. You use $$v_0$$ and $$a$$ to calculate the time it takes the car to complete the race. Both $$v_0$$ and $$a$$ have relative uncertainties of $$10\%,$$ and their uncertainties are independent.

Between the uncertainty in $$v_0$$ and the uncertainty in $$a,$$ which contributes greater uncertainty to your calculation of the time the car takes to complete the race?

choices.A: The uncertainty in $$v_0$$ for sufficiently short races and the uncertainty in $$a$$ for sufficiently long races.
choices.B: The uncertainty in $$v_0$$ for sufficiently long races and the uncertainty in $$a$$ for sufficiently short races.

problems.solution:
Let's think intuitively about this question. Two of the answer choices suggest that long and short races may be different from each other. It is usually easier to see and understand such differences if we think about the extremes.

Let's begin with an extremely short race. In this case, the race takes such a short time that the car's speed barely changes, simply because there is no time for the car to accelerate any significant amount. In that case, a $$10\%$$ error in $$v$$ contributes a $$10\%$$ error in the time to complete the race, but the error in the acceleration doesn't make any appreciable difference because there is no significant acceleration.

The race will be short like this when $$at \ll v_0,$$ with $$t$$ the time to complete the race. For such a race, $$t \approx l/v_0,$$ with $$l$$ the length of the race, so the race is short when $$al/v_0 \ll v_0,$$ or when $$l \ll \dfrac{v_0^2}{a}.$$ This calculation is not necessary to solve the question, but extends our understanding in case future questions ask about the length at which acceleration starts to matter.

Next, we imagine the race is very long, so $$at \gg v_0.$$ For example, suppose the car begins the race at $$v_0  = 0.01 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and finishes the race at $$v = 80 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Then the $$10\%$$ error in $$v_0$$ doesn't matter; it's the error in $$a$$ that affects our result.

This thought experiment shows that the answer is (a).

problems.statement:
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

In a certain batch of brass, the copper used had a density of $$8.96 \pm 0.19 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}.$$ The zinc had a density of $$7.14 \pm 0.30 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}.$$ The alloy was $$65.00 \pm 0.02 \%$$ copper by volume. These uncertainties are all independent. What was the uncertainty in the density of the resulting brass?

You may assume that in smelting, both volume and mass of metal are conserved.
problems.solution:
First, we notice that the relative error in the percentage of copper is very small compared to the other relative errors. This indicates that the uncertainty there can be ignored with minimal impact on our final results.

This problem involves error propagation, so we begin by searching for a formula on which to perform the error propagation.

The density of the alloy is a weighted average of the densities of the components. If the fraction of volume that is copper is $$\alpha,$$ then the density of the alloy is $$\rho = \alpha \rho_c + (1-\alpha) \rho_z.$$

The multiplication by factors $$\alpha$$ and $$(1-\alpha)$$ are examples of scaling a random variable. They do not change the relative error, and they multiply the absolute error by $$\alpha$$ and $$(1-\alpha)$$ respectively.

Using addition in quadrature, the total error is $$\sigma_\rho = \sqrt{(\alpha (\Delta \rho_c))^2 + \left((1-\alpha) (\Delta \rho_z) \right)^2}$$

Evaluating with the numbers given in the problem, the result is $$\Delta \rho = 0.16 \; \mathrm{ g/cm^3}.$$

problems.statement: A student makes an estimate of the acceleration due to gravity, $$g,$$ by dropping a rock from a known height $$h$$ and measuring the time $$t$$ it takes to hit the ground. Neglecting air resistance, which one of the following situations will lead to the smallest value of the relative uncertainty, $$\dfrac{\Delta g}{g},$$ in the estimate?

choices.A: There is no uncertainty in $$t$$ and $$h$$ has a $$10\%$$ uncertainty.
choices.B: There is no uncertainty in $$h$$ and $$t$$ has a $$10\%$$ uncertainty.
choices.D: (a) and (b) yield the same uncertainty, which is smaller than (c).
choices.E: (a), (b), and (c) all yield the same uncertainty.

problems.solution:
First, let's solve the short physics problem.

The distance fallen by an object with uniform acceleration $$a$$ is $$x = \dfrac12 at^2.$$ Substituting in $$h$$ for $$x$$ and $$g$$ for $$a,$$ we get $$h = \dfrac12 gt^2.$$ Solving for $$g,$$ $$g = \dfrac{2h}{t^2}$$

Next, we'll apply the rules for error propagation.

- Multiplying by a constant does not affect relative error
- When variables are multiplied, their relative errors add in quadrature.
- When variables are taken to some power, the relative error is $$\dfrac{\Delta(x^n)}{x^n} = |n| \dfrac{\Delta x}{x}.$$

Using the first of these rules, we ignore the $$2$$ in front of the right hand side of our equation.

Then applying the second rule, we have $$\left(\dfrac{\Delta g}{g}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{\Delta h}{h}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\Delta t^{-2}}{t^{-2}}\right)^2.$$
Applying the third rule, $$\left(\dfrac{\Delta g}{g}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{\Delta h}{h}\right)^2 + \left(2 \dfrac{\Delta t}{t}\right)^2$$

A relative error in $$t$$ contributes more uncertainty that a relative error in $$h.$$ This means (b), (d), and (e) are wrong.

Evaluating the equation for choices (a) and (c), we see that the error is smallest for choice (a).

problems.statement:
A car begins from rest and moves with constant acceleration $$a.$$ This fact is used to calculate the distance $$d$$ the car has traveled after a time $$t.$$

Which of the following is not true:

choices.A: If $$t$$ is uncertain by a fixed amount and $$a$$ is exact, the error in $$d$$ grows with $$t.$$
choices.B: If $$t$$ is uncertain by a fixed amount and $$a$$ is exact, the relative error in $$d$$ grows with $$t.$$
choices.C: If $$a$$ is uncertain by a fixed amount and $$t$$ is exact, the relative error in $$d$$ is constant over time.
choices.D: If both $$a$$ and $$t$$ are uncertain by 1%, the uncertainty in $$t$$ contributes more to the uncertainty in $$d$$ than the uncertainty in $$a$$ contributes.
choices.E: If $$t$$ is uncertain by 1% and $$a$$ is exact, the error in $$d$$ grows with $$t.$$

problems.solution:
The distance traveled is $$d = \dfrac12 at^2$$

Applying the rules for error propagation when quantities are multiplied and taken to a power, we have
$$ \left(\dfrac{\Delta d}{d}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{\Delta a}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{2\Delta t}{t}\right)^2$$

(a) says that if $$\Delta t$$ is fixed, $$\Delta d$$ increases with $$t.$$ Temporarily ignoring the error due to $$\Delta a$$ because it is not asked about in this part, we have $$\Delta d = \dfrac{2d}{t} \Delta t.$$ The quantity $$\dfrac{d}{t}$$ is the average speed, which increases with time, so $$\Delta d$$ increases with time. (a) is true.

(b) is false, since as $$t$$ increases, $$\dfrac{\Delta d}{d}$$ decreases. This is the answer. For completeness, we examine the remaining choices.

(c) is true because when $$\Delta t = 0,$$ the equation for the relative error in $$a$$ does not involve $$t.$$

(d) is also true. A percentage error is a relative error, and from the relative error formula we see a factor of $$2$$ multiplying the relative error in $$t,$$ but not in $$a,$$ indicating that $$t$$ contributes more relative error.

(e) In this scenario, $$\dfrac{\Delta t}{t}$$ is $$0.01,$$ meaning the relative error in $$d$$ is fixed over time. But because $$d$$ is growing, the __absolute__ error in $$d$$ is also growing, so this is true.

problems.statement:
Faith wants to measure the depth $$d$$ of a well. She decides to drop a stone into the well and measure the time $$t$$ until she hears the splash that the stone made at the bottom of the well. She models the fall of the stone accurately, but ignores the time it takes sound to travel back up the well.

Which of these is closest to the largest value of $$d$$ for which Faith will have less than a $$5\%$$ error in the depth measurement?

Take the speed of sound in air to be $$330 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$
problems.solution:
We will have to find an estimate for the depth of the well with and without the travel time included. Then we can demand that they differ by no more than $$5\%.$$

First, let's intuitively see why there is a largest depth of the well, instead of a smallest depth.

When should the time it takes sound to travel up the well matter? It matters when the stone's speed is not very small compared to the speed of sound. If the stone is always moving slowly compared to the speed of sound, the sound travel time will be very short compared to the stone travel time, and we can ignore the sound travel time with only a small error. However, if the stone falls at near the speed of sound, the time it takes sound to travel up the well is similar to the time it takes the stone to fall down the well, and ignoring sound creates a bad approximation.

The stone falls with constant acceleration, so $$d = \dfrac12 gt^2.$$ Using the rule for relative error with a variable to a power, $$\dfrac{\Delta d}{d} = 2\dfrac{\Delta t}{t} < 0.05$$

The sound takes a time $$\Delta t = \dfrac{d}{c}$$ to travel up the well, with $$c$$ the speed of sound. If we plug this in for $$\Delta t,$$ we get 
$$ 2\dfrac{d}{ct} < 0.05$$

Next we can take the time $$t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2d}{g}}$$ and plug it in. Simplifying, we get
$$ d < \dfrac{(0.05c)^2}{2g} .$$

Finally, putting in the numbers, we see $$d < 14 \;\mathrm{m}$$

problems.statement:
The King measures the length of his foot, determining it to within an error of $$\sigma_k.$$

Next, the Royal Measurer makes an independent measurement of The King's foot with an error of $$\sigma_m.$$

Both values are reported to the Royal Statistician, who explains that the uncertainty in the size of The King's foot is now $$\sigma_k/2.$$

Assuming the Royal Statistician accurately minimized the error in the reported length of The King's foot, what is the ratio $$\dfrac{\sigma_m}{\sigma_k}?$$
problems.solution:
When the Royal Statistician receives the measurements, they perform a weighted average,
$$ l = \alpha l_k + (1-\alpha) l_m,$$
where $$l_k$$ is the length measured by The King and $$l_m$$ is the length measured by the Royal Measurer. $$\alpha$$ is a number between $$0$$ and $$1.$$

The Royal Statistician chooses $$\alpha$$ so as to minimize the error. The error $$\sigma$$ in the weighted average, using addition in quadrature, is
$$\sigma^2 = \alpha^2 \sigma_k^2 + (1-\alpha)^2 \sigma_m^2.$$

This is a quadratic equation. As we saw in class $$\sigma$$ is minimized when 
$$\alpha = \dfrac{\sigma_m^2}{\sigma_k^2 + \sigma_m^2}$$ and the minimum error is
$$\sigma = \dfrac{(\sigma_m\sigma_k)}{\sqrt{\sigma_m^2 + \sigma_k^2}}.$$
We are told this minimum error is $$\sigma = \sigma_k/2.$$ Plugging this in and simplifying, we have
$$ \dfrac{\sigma_m}{\sqrt{\sigma_k^2 + \sigma_m^2}} = \dfrac12.$$
We can multiply both sides by $$\sqrt{\sigma_k^2 + \sigma_m^2}$$ and square to get
$$ \sigma_m^2 = \dfrac{\sigma_k^2 + \sigma_m^2}{4}.$$
Then we subtract $$\sigma_m^2/4$$ from both sides to obtain
$$\dfrac34 \sigma_m^2 = \dfrac14 \sigma_k^2.$$
Solving for $$\dfrac{\sigma_m}{\sigma_k},$$ we get
$$\dfrac{\sigma_m}{\sigma_k} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \approx 0.58.$$

problems.statement:
**a)** Galileo attempted to measure the speed of light. At night time, he stood on a hilltop while his assistant stood on another hilltop several miles away. Each had a lamp that was shielded (so that no one could see the light), but could be unshielded (at which point people could see the light it made). Galileo unshielded his lamp, and as soon as the assistant saw the light from Galileo's lamp, the assistant unshield his own lamp. Galileo recorded the time between unshielding his lamp and detecting light from his assistant's lamp. However, when using this method with distances up to five kilometers, Galileo could not detect any extra time delay.

If Galileo could measure times to within $$0.2\;\mathrm{s},$$ place a lower bound on the speed of light from Galileo's experiment.

**b)** The next improvement in measuring the speed of light was by Ole Rømer and others in 1676. Rømer observed Io, a moon of Jupiter. Due to its orbit, Io would disappear behind Jupiter from time to time, from the point of view of Earth. This is a very regular motion, but Rømer noticed that when Jupiter was far away from the Earth, Io emerged from eclipse later than when Jupiter was closer to Earth. Rømer was able to use observations of Io to estimate the time it takes light to travel from Earth to Jupiter. Then, using the known relative distances between the planets, he ultimately estimated that it takes light about 11 minutes to travel the Earth-Sun distance. His method was only accurate to 4 minutes.

Around the same time, the first estimates of the size of the solar system were made by measuring the parallax of Mars. These measurements estimated the Earth-Sun distance to be $$1.1 \times 10^{11}\;\mathrm{m},$$ accurate to about $$30\%.$$ What was the best estimate of the speed of light at this time? To about what accuracy was the speed of light known?

**c)** Today, the speed of light is set, by definition, to be 
$$c = 2.99792458 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$
This definition allows us to define the length one meter in terms of the duration one second. Because it is a definition, the error in $$c$$ is zero.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology claims that its best atomic clocks have an uncertainty of one second per 15 billion years. This is the best-known timekeeping in the world. What uncertainty does this imply over a length of $$4 \;\mathrm{km}?$$

**d)** The LIGO project has mirrors placed approximately $$4 \;\mathrm{km}$$ apart. In order to detect gravitational waves, the project attempts to measure displacements of mirrors on the order of $$10^{-19}\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Briefly explain how this is conceivably achievable, despite the limit described in part (c).

A plank rests on top of the axles of two identical wheels. Each wheel's outer radius is $$0.25 \;\mathrm{m},$$ and each wheel's axle has radius $$0.05 \;\mathrm{m}.$$ If the wheels roll $$1.00 \;\mathrm{m}$$ from their original position, how much does the plank move from its original position?

Assume that there is no slipping anywhere, and that the plank does not tip.
problems.solution:
Let $$R = 0.25\;\mathrm{m},$$ $$r = 0.05\;\mathrm{m},$$ and $$d = 1.00\;\mathrm{m}$$.

We know that the plank moves due to the translational motion of the wheels, but also due to the rotational motion of the wheels. For example, if you roll a book on top of a pencil, the pencil will eventually roll out from underneath the book.

To think about the amount the plank travels due to the rolling, let's consider the frame where the wheels do not have translational movement. In this frame, the wheels stay in place while the ground moves backwards a distance $$d$$. So, the wheel makes $$\frac{d}{2\pi R}$$ rotations. Since the plank rests on top of the axle with radius $$r$$, it travels a distance of $$\frac{d}{2\pi R} \cdot 2\pi r = \frac{dr}{R}$$ due to the rotation.

In the frame of the ground, we know that the wheels move a distance of $$d$$, so the total distance that the plank travels is
$$
 d + \frac{dr}{R} = d\left(1 + \frac{r}{R}\right) = \boxed{1.20 \;\mathrm{m}}.
$$

problems.statement: A uniform disk of mass $$M = 8.0 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ can rotate without friction on a fixed axis. A string is wrapped around its circumference and is attached to a $$m = 6.0 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ mass. The string does not slip. What is the tension in the cord while the mass is falling?
problems.solution:
We are given that the string does not slip on the disk, which gives us a way to relate the angular acceleration of the wheel and the acceleration of the mass attached to the end of the string.

Let $$T$$ be the tension in the string and $$r$$ the radius of the disk. We can draw a diagram with forces:

Since the string does not slip, we have $$\alpha = \frac{a}{r}.$$ Considering the torque of the disk,
$$
 \tau = I \alpha = T r
 \implies \frac{1}{2} M r^2 \frac{a}{r} = T r
 \implies \frac{1}{2} M a = T.
$$
Considering the acceleration on the hanging mass,
$$
 mg - T = ma
 \implies a = g - \frac{T}{m}.
$$
Substituting this into the equation we obtained from torque,
$$
 T = \frac{1}{2} M \left(g - \frac{T}{m}\right)
 \implies M(mg - T) = 2Tm
 \implies Mmg = 2Tm + TM.
$$
Solving for $$T$$,
$$
 T = \frac{Mmg}{2m + M} = 24.0 \;\mathrm{N}.
$$

problems.statement: A uniform circular disk of radius $$R$$ begins with a mass $$M.$$ A hole is cut in the disk as shown in the diagram. In terms of the radius $$R$$ and the mass $$M$$ of the original disk, what is the moment of inertia of the resulting object about the same axis? The moment of inertia about an axis through the center of the disk and perpendicular to the plane of the disk is $$I_0 = \frac{1}{2} M R^2.$$
problems.solution:
Here we notice that we can add the missing circle to the final object to get the full circle, which is easier to find the moment of inertial of. In particular, we have the following equation relating the moments of inertia:

We know that the moment of inertia of the full disk is $$\tfrac{1}{2} M R^2.$$ We also know that the small disk has half of the big circle's radius, so its area, and therefore mass, is $$\tfrac{1}{4}$$ of the full disk's. Therefore, the moment of inertia of the small disk about its own center is $$\tfrac{1}{2} (\tfrac{M}{4})(\tfrac{R}{2})^2 = \tfrac{1}{32} MR^2.$$ However, we are interested in the moment of inertia about a point on the edge of the disk. We can use the parallel axis theorem for this. The point we are interested in is a distance of $$\tfrac{R}{2}$$ away from the center of mass, so the new moment of inertia is
$$
    \frac{1}{32} MR^2 + \frac{M}{4} \left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{3}{32} MR^2.
$$
Therefore, our equation becomes
$$
    \frac{3}{32} MR^2 + I = \frac{1}{2} MR^2 \implies I = \boxed{\frac{13}{32} MR^2}.
$$

Source: F=ma 2010 #24

problems.statement: A person of mass $$M_2$$ stands on the edge of a disk of mass $$M_1$$ and radius $$R$$. The disk can rotate freely about its center without friction, and there is enough friction between the disk and the person so that the person rotates with the disk. The disk and person are initially stationary. If the person then throws a stone of mass $$m$$ in the direction tangent to the disk's edge with initial velocity $$v$$ relative to the center of the disk, what is the angular speed $$\omega$$ of the disk/person system about the center of the disk immediately after the stone is thrown?
problems.solution:
This situation is the rotational version of throwing a stone while on a frictionless surface. We'll use conservation of angular momentum to find the angular velocity.

Before the person throws the stone, the total angular momentum of the system is $$0$$, because nothing is moving.

The moment of inertia of the person and the disk is $$\frac{1}{2} M_1R^2 + M_2 R^2$$, the sum of their individual moments of inertia.

After the person throws the stone, the stone has an angular momentum of $$|\vec r \times \vec p| = mvR$$. The angular momentum of the person and disk is $$I\omega$$, where $$I = \frac{1}{2} M_1 R^2 + M_2 R^2$$. Therefore, we have
$$
 0 = mvR + \left(\frac{1}{2} M_1 R^2 + M_2 R^2 \right)\omega \implies \omega = \boxed{\frac{2mv}{R(M_1 + 2M_2)}}.
$$

We have ignored the minus sign on $$\omega$$ because the problem asks for an angular speed, which is the absolute value of angular velocity.

Source: AP Physics C 2014 FRQ #3

problems.statement: Two disks are mounted on thin, lightweight rods oriented through their centers and normal to the disks. These axles are constrained to be vertical at all times, and the disks can pivot frictionlessly on the rods. The disks have identical thickness and are made of the same material, but have differing radii $$r_1$$ and $$r_2$$. The disks are given angular velocities of magnitudes $$\omega_1$$ and $$\omega_2$$ respectively, and are brought into contact at their edges. After the disks interact via friction, it is found that both disks come exactly to a halt. Which of the following must hold? Ignore effects associated with the vertical rods.
problems.solution:
It's tempting to try angular momentum conservation here. If we define a system to consist of two disks and two rods, then the friction forces between the disks are internal forces; they don't change the system's angular momentum. However, if there's a friction force on the disk $$1,$$ and the disk doesn't start accelerating, it means there is also some constraint force on it. This force comes from the rod, which is connected to something else that holds the rod in place. The constraint forces holding everything in place are external to the system, and since they're applied one on the rod $$1$$ and one on rod $$2,$$ they exert net torque on the system, regardless of where we define the origin. This means we can't solve the problem with angular momentum conservation.

Instead, we'll find how much angular momentum each disk loses.

With a friction force $$F$$ on its edge, a disk experiences a torque about its center of

$$ \tau = Fr\,.$$

The angular momentum lost by a disk is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta L & = \tau \cdot \Delta t \\
{} & = F r \Delta t.
\end{aligned}
$$

The disks stop at the same moment, since if they did not and one disk stopped first, the other disk would start it spinning again, and we wouldn't find that both disks eventually come to a complete halt, as the problem states.

Since $$F$$ and $$\Delta t$$ are the same for each disk, let's rewrite the previous equation as
$$ F \Delta t = \dfrac{\Delta L}{r}$$
to get a quantity that is the same for each disk.

Since both disks come to a stop, $$\Delta L$$ is equal in magnitude to the initial angular momentum of the disk. The angular momentum is $$L = \dfrac12 m r^2 \omega.$$ The mass of each disk is proportional to $$r^2,$$ so $$L \propto r^4 \omega.$$

Since $$\dfrac{L}{r}$$ is the same for each disk, we have that $$\dfrac{r^4 \omega}{r}$$ is the same for each disk, or

$$ \boxed{\omega_1 r_1^3 = \omega_2 r_2^3\,.}$$

Source: 2009 F=ma #25

problems.statement: The moment of inertia of a uniform equilateral triangle with mass $$m$$ and side length $$a$$ about an axis through one of its sides and parallel to that side is $$(1/8) ma^2$$. What is the moment of inertia of a uniform regular hexagon of mass $$m$$ and side length $$a$$ about an axis through two opposite vertices?
problems.solution:
In this problem, we're given a moment of inertia of an equilateral triangle, and we want to find the moment of inertia of a regular hexagon. Since a regular hexagon can be thought of as a composition of six equilateral triangles, we expect to use both the parallel axis theorem and the additivity of moments of inertia.
